Extremal distance spectral radius of graphs with fixed size

Hongying Lin Note: E-mail: linhy99@scut.edu.cn Affiliation: School of Mathematics, South China University of TechnologyGuangzhou 510641, P.R. China    Bo Zhou Note: E-mail: zhoubo@m.scnu.edu.cn Affiliation: School of Mathematical Sciences, South China Normal UniversityGuangzhou 510631, P.R. China
Abstract

Let mm be a positive integer. Brualdi and Hoffman proposed the problem to determine the (connected) graphs with maximum spectral radius in a given graph class and they posed a conjecture for the class of graphs with given size mm. After partial results due to Friedland and Stanley, Rowlinson completely confirmed the conjecture. The distance spectral radius of a connected graph is the largest eigenvalue of its distance matrix. We investigate the problem to determine the connected graphs with minimum distance spectral radius in the class of graphs with size mm. Given mm, there is exactly one positive integer nn such that (n−12)<m≤(n2){n-1\choose 2}<m\leq{n\choose 2}. We establish some structural properties of the extremal graphs for all mm and solve the problem for (n−12)+max⁡{n−62,1}≤m≤(n2){n-1\choose 2}+\max\{\frac{n-6}{2},1\}\leq m\leq{n\choose 2}. We give a conjecture for the remaining case. To prove the main results, we also determine the the complements of forests of fixed order with large and small distance spectral radius.

MSC: 05C12, 05C50, 15A48

Key words: distance spectral radius, complement of a forest, graph size

1 Introduction

Throughout this paper, we consider simple graphs. Let GG be a connected graph with vertex set V⁡(G)V(G) and edge set E⁡(G)E(G). Denote m⁡(G)m(G) the size of GG. The distance between vertices u,v∈V⁡(G)u,v\in V(G), denoted by dG​(u,v)d_{G}(u,v), is the length of a shortest path between them. The distance matrix of GG, denoted by D⁡(G)D(G), is the matrix D⁡(G)=(dG​(u,v))u,v∈V⁡(G)D(G)=(d_{G}(u,v))_{u,v\in V(G)}. Since D⁡(G)D(G) is real and symmetric, its eigenvalues are all real. The distance spectral radius of GG, denoted by ρ⁡(G)\rho(G), is the largest eigenvalue of D⁡(G)D(G). For |V⁡(G)|≥2|V(G)|\geq 2, since D⁡(G)D(G) is irreducible, we have by the Perron-Frobenius theorem that ρ⁡(G)\rho(G) is simple and positive, and there is a unique positive unit eigenvector x⁡(G)x(G) of D⁡(G)D(G) corresponding to ρ⁡(G)\rho(G), which we call the distance Perron vector of GG.

The study of eigenvalues of the distance matrix of a connected graph dates back to the classical work of Graham and Pollak [10], Graham and Lovász [9] and Edelberg et al. [7]. The distance spectral radius was used as a molecular descriptor [3]. Ruzieh and Powers [17] and Stevanović and Ilić [19] showed that among the connected graphs of order nn, the complete graph KnK_{n} is the unique graph with minimum distance spectral radius, while the path PnP_{n} is the unique graph with maximum distance spectral radius, where the uniqueness of the path was established in [19]. Related to many problems and properties of graphs such as Laplacian spectral properties [14] and graph parameters based on distance [2], the distance eigenvalues and especially of the distance spectral radius received much attention, see the surveys [1, 12] (and the references therein) and the very recent [5]. We mention that such research was also extended to Laplacian and signless Laplacian versions [16], hypergraphs [21] and other distances such as Steiner distance [6].

Let mm be a positive integer. There is exactly one positive integer nn such that (n−12)<m≤(n2){n-1\choose 2}<m\leq{n\choose 2}. It is easily seen that 1+8​m2≤n<3+8​m+12\frac{1+\sqrt{8m}}{2}\leq n<\frac{3+\sqrt{8m+1}}{2}. Thus n=⌈1+8​m2⌉n=\left\lceil\frac{1+\sqrt{8m}}{2}\right\rceil. After showing that the maximum adjacency spectral radius of a graph with (n2){n\choose 2} edges, n≥2n\geq 2, is n−1n-1, with equality precisely when the only nontrivial component of the graph is KnK_{n}, Brualdi and Hoffman conjectured that among all graphs with mm edges, (n−12)<m<(n2){n-1\choose 2}<m<{n\choose 2}, the maximal index is attained precisely when the only nontrivial component is the graph obtained from Kn−1K_{n-1} by adding one new vertex of degree m−(n−12)m-{n-1\choose 2}. Friedland [8] and Stanley [18] gave some partial results on this conjecture, which was confirmed finally by Rowlinson [15]. Let 𝔾⁡(m)\mathbb{G}(m) be the set of connected graphs with mm edges. Evidently, 𝔾⁡(m)={Pm+1}\mathbb{G}(m)=\{P_{m+1}\} when m=1,2m=1,2. Thus, we assume in the following that m≥3m\geq 3. Then m=(n−12)+sm={n-1\choose 2}+s with 1≤s≤n−11\leq s\leq n-1. So the graph GmG_{m} obtained from Kn−1K_{n-1} by adding a new vertex of degree ss is the unique graph achieving the maximum adjacency spectral radius.

In this paper, we study the following problem.

Problem 1.1.

Determine the graphs in 𝔾⁡(m)\mathbb{G}(m) with maximum and minimum distance spectral radius.

It turns out that the maximum part is easy. However, the minimum is much more difficult. By existing results and experiments, the graphs with maximum (minimum, resp.) adjacency spectral radius happen to be the graphs with minimum (maximum, resp.) distance spectral radius over many classes of graphs, including trees and graphs with given parameters such as order, connectivity, clique number, etc. Our results show that this is not the case in the class 𝔾⁡(m)\mathbb{G}(m) for s<n−2s<n-2. The main results are listed below.

For integer n≥4n\geq 4, let AnA_{n} be the tree obtained from a path v1​…​vn−1v_{1}\ldots v_{n-1} by add a new vertex vnv_{n} and a new edge vn​v2v_{n}v_{2}. For integer n≥6n\geq 6, let BnB_{n} be the tree obtained from a path v1​…​vn−1v_{1}\ldots v_{n-1} by add a new vertex vnv_{n} and a new edge vn​v3v_{n}v_{3}.

Theorem 1.1.

Let G∈𝔾⁡(m)∖{Pm+1,Am+1}G\in\mathbb{G}(m)\setminus\{P_{m+1},A_{m+1}\}, where m≥5m\geq 5. Then ρ⁡(G)≤ρ⁡(Bm+1)<ρ⁡(Am+1)<ρ⁡(Pm+1)\rho(G)\leq\rho(B_{m+1})<\rho(A_{m+1})<\rho(P_{m+1}) with equality in the first inequality if and only if G≅Bm+1G\cong B_{m+1}.

For a graph GG, we denote by G¯\overline{G} the complement of GG. Let Δ⁡(G)\Delta(G) and δ⁡(G)\delta(G) be the maximum degree and minimum degree of a graph GG, respectively.

For positive integers n≥2n\geq 2 and 1≤c≤n1\leq c\leq n, write

Pn,c=(c+c⁡⌊nc⌋−n)​P⌊nc⌋∪(n−c⁡⌊nc⌋)​P⌈nc⌉¯.P_{n,c}=\overline{\left(c+c\lfloor\tfrac{n}{c}\rfloor-n\right)P_{\lfloor\frac{n}{c}\rfloor}\cup\left(n-c\lfloor\tfrac{n}{c}\rfloor\right)P_{\lceil\frac{n}{c}\rceil}}\,.

Obviously, Pn,1=Pn¯P_{n,1}=\overline{P_{n}} and Pn,n=KnP_{n,n}=K_{n}.

Theorem 1.2.

Let G∈𝔾⁡(m)G\in\mathbb{G}(m), n=⌈1+8​m2⌉n=\left\lceil\frac{1+\sqrt{8m}}{2}\right\rceil and s=m−(n−12)s=m-{n-1\choose 2}, where m≥3m\geq 3. Suppose that ρ⁡(G)\rho(G) is as small as possible. Then the order of GG is nn, and

  1. (i)

    if s≥n−12s\geq\frac{n-1}{2}, then Δ⁡(G)=n−1\Delta(G)=n-1;

  2. (ii)

    if s=n−22s=\frac{n-2}{2} and nn is even, then Δ⁡(G)=δ⁡(G)=n−2\Delta(G)=\delta(G)=n-2;

  3. (iii)

    if 1≤s<n−221\leq s<\frac{n-2}{2}, then Δ⁡(G)=n−2\Delta(G)=n-2 and δ⁡(G)=n−3\delta(G)=n-3, i.e., each component of G¯\overline{G} is either a cycle or a nontrivial paths, and there are exactly s+1s+1 components being paths in G¯\overline{G}.

Theorem 1.3.

Let G∈𝔾⁡(m)G\in\mathbb{G}(m), n=⌈1+8​m2⌉n=\left\lceil\frac{1+\sqrt{8m}}{2}\right\rceil and s=m−(n−12)s=m-{n-1\choose 2}, where m≥3m\geq 3. If max⁡{n−62,1}≤s≤n−1\max\{\frac{n-6}{2},1\}\leq s\leq n-1, then ρ⁡(G)≥ρ⁡(Pn,s+1)\rho(G)\geq\rho(P_{n,s+1}) with equality if and only if G≅Pn,s+1G\cong P_{n,s+1}.

To obtain these results, we also study the graphs which are the complements of forests with large and small distance spectral radius, respectively. At the end of the paper, we propose a conjecture on the extremal graphs for s<n−62s<\frac{n-6}{2}.

2 Preliminaries

Let GG be a connected graph with V⁡(G)={v1,…,vn}V(G)=\{v_{1},\dots,v_{n}\}. A column vector x=(xv1,…,xvn)⊤∈ℝnx=(x_{v_{1}},\dots,x_{v_{n}})^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{n} (whether it is the distance Perron vector of GG or not) can be considered as a function defined on V⁡(G)V(G) which maps vertex viv_{i} to xvix_{v_{i}}, i.e., x⁡(vi)=xvix(v_{i})=x_{v_{i}} for i=1,…,ni=1,\dots,n. Then

x⊤​D​(G)​x=∑{u,v}⊆V⁡(G)2​dG​(u,v)​xu​xv.x^{\top}D(G)x=\sum_{\{u,v\}\subseteq V(G)}2d_{G}(u,v)x_{u}x_{v}.

For a unit column vector x∈ℝnx\in\mathbb{R}^{n} with at least one nonnegative entry, by Rayleigh’s principle, we have

ρ⁡(G)≥x⊤​D​(G)​x\rho(G)\geq x^{\top}D(G)x

with equality if and only if xx is the distance Perron vector of GG. In this case,

ρ⁡(G)​xu=∑v∈V⁡(G)dG​(u,v)​xv,\rho(G)x_{u}=\sum_{v\in V(G)}d_{G}(u,v)x_{v},

which we call the (ρ⁡(G),x)(\rho(G),x)-eigenequation (at uu).

For a connected graph GG with v∈V⁡(G)v\in V(G), let δG​(v)\delta_{G}(v) be the degree of vv in GG, NG​(v)N_{G}(v) the set of neighbors of vv in GG, and T​rG​(v)=∑w∈V⁡(G)dG​(v,w)Tr_{G}(v)=\sum_{w\in V(G)}d_{G}(v,w), which is the transmission of vv in GG. The Wiener index is the sum of the distances between all vertex pairs in GG, i.e., W⁡(G)=12​∑v∈V⁡(G)T​rG​(v)W(G)=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{v\in V(G)}Tr_{G}(v). If the transmissions of all vertices in GG are equal, then we say GG is transmission regular.

Let SnS_{n} and CnC_{n} be the star and the cycle on nn vertices, respectively.

Let GG be a connected graph. For ∅≠V1⊂V⁡(G)\emptyset\neq V_{1}\subset V(G), G⁡[V1]G[V_{1}] denotes the subgraph of GG induced by V1V_{1}. For E1⊆E⁡(G)E_{1}\subseteq E(G), G−E1G-E_{1} denotes the graph obtained from GG by deleting all edges of E1E_{1}. If E1={u​v}E_{1}=\{uv\}, then we write G−u​vG-uv for G−{u​v}G-\{uv\}. If E′E^{\prime} is a subset of edges of the complement of GG, then G+E′G+E^{\prime} denotes the graph obtained from GG by inserting all edges of E′E^{\prime}. If E′={u​v}E^{\prime}=\{uv\}, then we write G+u​vG+uv for G+{u​v}G+\{uv\}.

The following lemma is an immediate consequence of the Perron-Frobenius theorem.

Lemma 2.1.

[17] Let G be a connected graph with {u,v}⊂V⁡(G)\{u,v\}\subset V(G). If u​v∉E⁡(G)uv\not\in E(G), then ρ⁡(G)>ρ⁡(G+u​v)\rho(G)>\rho(G+uv).

Lemma 2.2.

[20] Let GG be a connected graph of order nn, and T​rmin​(G)Tr_{\min}(G) and T​rmax​(G)Tr_{\max}(G) be the minimum transmission of GG and the maximum transmission, respectively. Then T​rmin​(G)≤ρ⁡(G)≤T​rmax​(G)Tr_{\min}(G)\leq\rho(G)\leq Tr_{\max}(G) and ρ⁡(G)≥2​W​(G)n\rho(G)\geq\frac{2W(G)}{n} with either equality if and only if GG is transmission regular.

Lemma 2.3.

[22] For a connected graph GG with η\eta being an automorphism of GG and x=x⁡(G)x=x(G), η⁡(vi)=vj\eta(v_{i})=v_{j} implies that xi=xjx_{i}=x_{j}.

Lemma 2.4.

Let GG be a graph of diameter 22 with x=x⁡(G)x=x(G). Let {u,v}⊂V⁡(G)\{u,v\}\subset V(G) with ∅≠S⊆NG​(u)∖({v}∪NG​(v))\emptyset\neq S\subseteq N_{G}(u)\setminus(\{v\}\cup N_{G}(v)). Let G′=G−{u​w:w∈S}+{v​w:w∈S}G^{\prime}=G-\{uw:w\in S\}+\{vw:w\in S\}. If xu≥xvx_{u}\geq x_{v} and the diameter of G′G^{\prime} is also two, then ρ⁡(G′)>ρ⁡(G)\rho(G^{\prime})>\rho(G).

Proof.

Note that diameters of GG and G′G^{\prime} are two. As we pass from GG to G′G^{\prime}, the distance between a vertex of SS and vv is decreased by 11, the distance between a vertex of SS and uu is increased by 11, and the distance between any other vertex pair remains unchanged. Thus, we have by Rayleigh’s principle that

12​(ρ⁡(G′)−ρ⁡(G))≥12​x⊤​(D⁡(G′)−D⁡(G))​x=∑w∈Sxw​(xu−xv)≥0,\frac{1}{2}(\rho(G^{\prime})-\rho(G))\geq\frac{1}{2}x^{\top}(D(G^{\prime})-D(G))x=\sum_{w\in S}x_{w}(x_{u}-x_{v})\geq 0,

so ρ⁡(G′)≥ρ⁡(G)\rho(G^{\prime})\geq\rho(G). If ρ⁡(G′)=ρ⁡(G)\rho(G^{\prime})=\rho(G), then ρ⁡(G′)=x⊤​D​(G′)​x\rho(G^{\prime})=x^{\top}D(G^{\prime})x, so xx is also the distance Perron vector of G′G^{\prime}. Then, from the (ρ⁡(G),x)(\rho(G),x)-eigenequation and the (ρ⁡(G′),x)(\rho(G^{\prime}),x)-eigenequation at uu, we have

0=ρ⁡(G′)​xu−ρ⁡(G)​xu=∑w∈Sxw>0,0=\rho(G^{\prime})x_{u}-\rho(G)x_{u}=\sum_{w\in S}x_{w}>0,

a contradiction. It follows that ρ⁡(G′)>ρ⁡(G)\rho(G^{\prime})>\rho(G). ∎

A vertex of a graph is known as a pendant vertex or a leaf if it is degree is one. An edge incident to such a vertex is a pendant edge; otherwise, it is a non-pendant edge.

3 Graphs which are the complements of forests with large and small distance spectral radius

If GG is a graph and u​vuv is an edge of GG that is not a cut edge, then we denote by G⁡(u​v)G(uv) the graph obtained from GG by identifying the vertices uu and vv as vertex uu, and adding a new pendent edge u​vuv.

Lemma 3.1.

Let GG be the complement of the union of cc disjoint graphs G1,…,GcG_{1},\ldots,G_{c} of orders n1,…,ncn_{1},\ldots,n_{c}, respectively, where c≥2c\geq 2. If G1G_{1} is a tree with a non-pendant edge u​vuv, then ρ⁡(G)<ρ⁡(G1​(u​v)∪G2∪⋯∪Gc¯)\rho(G)<\rho\left(\overline{G_{1}(uv)\cup G_{2}\cup\cdots\cup G_{c}}\right).

Proof.

Let G′=G1​(u​v)∪G2∪⋯∪Gc¯G^{\prime}=\overline{G_{1}(uv)\cup G_{2}\cup\cdots\cup G_{c}}. Obviously, the diameter of G′G^{\prime} is two. Let x=x⁡(G)x=x(G). Suppose without loss of generality that xu≥xvx_{u}\geq x_{v}. By Lemma 2.4, ρ⁡(G′)>ρ⁡(G)\rho(G^{\prime})>\rho(G). ∎

A tree of order nn with diameter three is a double star Dn,aD_{n,a}, obtainable by adding an edge between the centers of two disjoint stars Sa+1S_{a+1} and Sn−a−1S_{n-a-1} for some aa with 2​a≤n−22a\leq n-2.

Lin and Drury [11] proved among the graphs of order nn whose complements are trees different from the star, Dn,1D_{n,1} and PnP_{n} are the graphs achieving maximum and minimum distance spectral radius, respectively. We establish results of the complements of forests.

Let GG be the complement of a forest on nn vertices with cc components, where c≥2c\geq 2. If G≇Sn−c+1∪(c−1)​K1¯G\ncong\overline{S_{n-c+1}\cup(c-1)K_{1}}, then

with equality in the first inequality if and only if G¯≅Dn−c+1,1∪(c−1)​K1\overline{G}\cong D_{n-c+1,1}\cup(c-1)K_{1}.

By Lemma 3.1, ρ⁡(Sn−c+1∪(c−1)​K1¯)>ρ⁡(Dn−c+1,1∪(c−1)​K1¯)\rho(\overline{S_{n-c+1}\cup(c-1)K_{1}})>\rho(\overline{D_{n-c+1,1}\cup(c-1)K_{1}}).

Case 2. n2=1n_{2}=1.

Note that c≤n−3c\leq n-3 as G≇Sn−c+1∪(c−1)​K1¯G\ncong\overline{S_{n-c+1}\cup(c-1)K_{1}}.

Claim 3.3.

T1T_{1} is a double star.

Proof.

Suppose that T1T_{1} is not a double star. Then the diameter of T1T_{1} is at least 44. Let v0​v1​…​vdv_{0}v_{1}\ldots v_{d} be a diametral path in T1T_{1}, where d≥4d\geq 4. T1′=T1−{w​v2:w∈NT1​(v2)∖{v1}}+{w​v3:w∈NT1​(v2)∖{v1}}T^{\prime}_{1}=T_{1}-\{wv_{2}:w\in N_{T_{1}}(v_{2})\setminus\{v_{1}\}\}+\{wv_{3}:w\in N_{T_{1}}(v_{2})\setminus\{v_{1}\}\}

if xv2≤xv3x_{v_{2}}\leq x_{v_{3}} and

7 Concluding remarks

By Theorem 1.3, the graph Pn,s+1P_{n,s+1} uniquely minimizes the distance spectral radius among 𝔾⁡(m)\mathbb{G}(m), where n=⌈1+8​m2⌉n=\left\lceil\frac{1+\sqrt{8m}}{2}\right\rceil, s=m−(n−12)s=m-{n-1\choose 2}, and max⁡{n−62,1}≤s≤n−1\max\{\frac{n-6}{2},1\}\leq s\leq n-1. The two smallest cases not covered by Theorem 1.3 is (m,n,s)=(29,9,1)(m,n,s)=(29,9,1) and (m,n,s)=(37,10,1)(m,n,s)=(37,10,1). Let GG be a graph satisfying the conditions in Theorem 1.2. For the former (latter, respectively) case, the possible graph GG and the the value of ρ⁡(G)\rho(G) are listed in Table 1 (Table 2, respectively). From the two tables, we find that Pn,s+1P_{n,s+1} uniquely minimizes the distance spectral radius. Based on these observations further computer searching results, So we pose the following conjecture:

Let G∈𝔾⁡(m)G\in\mathbb{G}(m), n=⌈1+8​m2⌉n=\left\lceil\frac{1+\sqrt{8m}}{2}\right\rceil and s=m−(n−12)s=m-{n-1\choose 2}, where m≥3m\geq 3 and 1≤s≤n−621\leq s\leq\frac{n-6}{2}. Then ρ⁡(G)≥ρ⁡(Pn,s+1)\rho(G)\geq\rho(P_{n,s+1}) with equality if and only if G≅Pn,s+1G\cong P_{n,s+1}. If it is true, then by Theorem 3.2, to prove the conjecture, it suffices to show that each component of G¯\overline{G} is a tree.
